candidateAnswers.argumentAgainst: Every town gets the same mix, which is the single national average the owner has asked us to avoid where better is available.
candidateAnswers.argumentFor: One national table is quick and sourced.
candidateAnswers.label: One national household-type table
candidateAnswers.position: Use the Census Bureau's national shares of household types, sizes and ages of members.

candidateAnswers.argumentAgainst: More data to carry, one row per state or county.
candidateAnswers.argumentFor: A retirement town, a college town and a suburb would start with the households they really have.
candidateAnswers.label: Household-type shares by state or county
candidateAnswers.position: Use the ACS household-type table for the town's state or county, falling back to the national one.

notes: Built 2026-09-23 on branch claude/project-thread-l04zry-residents: src/simulation/living-world/town-residents.ts seats up to 40 households in the player's town at the start of a game. The shares it uses are marked placeholders: 28% one person alone, 30% a couple with no children at home, 20% a couple with children, 10% one parent with children, 12% unrelated housemates; one to three children; every couple recorded as married; adult ages drawn evenly within a band. None of these came from a source.
The employed share of adults (59.7%, BLS CPS 2025 annual average, Table 57) is sourced and is not part of this question.
question: What share of American households are (a) one person living alone, (b) a married couple with no children under 18 at home, (c) a married couple with children under 18, (d) an unmarried couple, with and without children, (e) a single parent with children under 18, and (f) other non-family households such as roommates? For each, what is the usual number of children and the age distribution of the householder? Nationally from the latest ACS 1-year tables, and by state (or county) where the table exists.
